The machinist was freeing a seized clamping lever on the vertical mill at the start of a setup. The task was a response to a fault, jam or alarm. Stage of the task: setup or preparation. Method in effect: SW-612 Vertical Mill Fixture Changeover. The task was not being performed as written. The difference from the written method was as follows: the written method says a seized lever is reported to maintenance rather than freed by hand, but the job was due to run that shift so it was pulled by hand first. Equipment involved: Vertical mill VM-07, fixture clamping lever. Equipment state at the time: de-energized and at rest or stopped. Equipment condition: known fault already reported. Detail: The clamping lever has been stiff for several weeks and is on the maintenance backlog. PPE in use: safety glasses and general purpose gloves. This matched the PPE specified for the task. The event was not witnessed and was self reported at the time. Immediately before the event: standing square to the mill with the right hand on the clamping lever at about shoulder height and the left hand braced on the machine table. Body position at the moment: standing upright. At the moment of the event: a hard pull was applied to the lever, the lever gave suddenly and the right arm travelled back and up past shoulder height, at which point a sharp pain was felt in the front of the right shoulder. Immediately after the event: the machinist let go of the lever, stepped back from the mill holding the right arm against the body, and called the team lead. The prior condition relates to a previous work-related case at this site. Change in the condition: The previously repaired right shoulder had full range of motion and no symptoms before this. After the lever gave, the arm could not be raised above shoulder height and the pain has been constant since. The injury arose from overexertion during manual handling. Load handled: no discrete weight - a push, pull or jammed part. The load was moved from shoulder height to above shoulder or overhead. It was held at full extended reach. Assist device: An assist device was available but not used. This was a push, pull or carry rather than a lift. Point of contact: front of the right shoulder. Force applied from behind. Difference from a normal run of this task: The lever had been stiff for weeks but gave suddenly on this occasion rather than freeing gradually. Conditions at the point of injury: nothing notable. The event occurred in the first hour of the shift. No overtime was being worked. It happened within the first few minutes. The machinist had performed this task before. A known hazard, prior near miss, open action or risk assessment covers this task. Detail: The stiff clamping lever on VM-07 has been on the maintenance backlog for about six weeks and a work order is open. No guard, interlock, barrier or control was bypassed, missing, defeated or ineffective. Stop-work opportunity: The lever could have been reported to maintenance as the written method requires, but the job was due to run that shift and the wait was expected to be long. At the scene, a cold pack was applied. This was given by a trained first aid responder. Notified: the team lead and EHS. This happened within a few minutes. Afterwards, the equipment was stopped. Work at the location stopped. The machinist was sent to an offsite occupational clinic for evaluation.
